strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for multimodal NLP: whether chart-question-answering systems remain reliable when visual design distorts the apparent meaning of data.

Evaluation covers 18 models, 17 misleader categories, and both synthetic and real-world examples. CHARTOM’s paired misleading and non-misleading visualizations provide particularly useful evidence of susceptibility.

The mitigation experiments report substantial improvements from table-based QA (15.4–19.6 percentage points) and significant improvements from redrawing for two models. Evaluating effects on non-misleading charts is an important strength.
The presentation is generally clear, with informative examples and useful discussion of extraction failures, oracle misleader labels, and limitations of chart redrawing.
weaknesses: The central claim of improvement without compromising non-misleading accuracy is not established. Table-based QA significantly reduces that accuracy for two models, while Figure 7 shows decreases for all three models under redrawing. Nonsignificant decreases do not demonstrate preservation; confidence intervals and a justified noninferiority analysis are needed. Correction methods are also not evaluated on ChartQA.

Reproducibility is insufficient in the submitted manuscript. The promised code/data footnote is blank, and exact prompts, model/API versions, answer-parsing rules, free-text and ranking scoring procedures, and the calculation of the 25.6% random baseline are missing. These details are especially consequential because the evaluation mixes multiple-choice, free-text, and ranking questions.

The headline accuracy drops compare datasets that differ in questions, chart composition, and provenance, so the aggregate differences cannot be attributed solely to misleading design. CHARTOM provides a matched comparison and supports the qualitative vulnerability finding, but this should be the primary controlled analysis, with paired uncertainty estimates and results by question format.

The mitigation comparisons do not isolate why table-based QA works: this condition switches the answerer to Qwen2.5-7B, whereas image-plus-table conditions retain the original MLLM. A same-model table-only control is needed before attributing the difference specifically to removing the image. Comparisons with established plot-to-table or simplification approaches, such as the cited DePlot and SimPlot, would also clarify the contribution.

Several generalizations exceed the available evidence. Experiment 2 contains only four chart pairs, with significance assessed across related models rather than independent chart examples. Some misleader categories contain only one instance. Numerous significance tests are reported without a stated multiplicity treatment, and correction experiments cover only three models selected from those performing below chance.

The 42 newly annotated real-world examples lack a documented selection and validation protocol, including how correct answers were verified and ambiguities resolved. The explanation that parametric knowledge protects models is plausible but untested without question-only or altered-label controls. Likewise, extracted-table agreement is not extraction accuracy, and the definitions of perfect and partial matching are unspecified.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for multimodal NLP: whether chart-question-answering systems remain reliable when visual design distorts the apparent meaning of data. Evaluating both vulnerabilities and practical mitigation methods gives the study a useful, coherent aim.

The evaluation spans 18 models, general-purpose and chart-specialized systems, and 17 categories of misleading visualization. Combining existing assessments with 42 newly annotated real-world examples provides useful breadth.

The correction experiments provide promising evidence: table-based QA improves accuracy by 15.4–19.6 percentage points on misleading examples, and redrawing significantly improves two of the three evaluated models. Evaluating ordinary charts as well exposes an important trade-off.
The presentation is generally clear, with informative examples and explicit discussion of extraction errors, failed rendering, and the limitations of warnings that assume known misleader labels.
weaknesses: The headline claim of improving robustness without compromising ordinary-chart accuracy is not established. Table-based QA significantly reduces non-misleading accuracy for two models, by up to 8.5 percentage points. Redrawing also has negative point estimates for all three models in Figure 7; nonsignificant decreases do not demonstrate preservation. Confidence intervals and a justified noninferiority margin are needed, preferably with correction methods also evaluated on the larger ChartQA benchmark.

The main aggregate vulnerability comparison confounds misleading design with dataset composition and difficulty. The misleading and non-misleading collections contain different sources and questions, while ChartQA also differs in response format. CHARTOM provides a useful paired subset and its reported results support vulnerability, but the aggregate 23.4-point and 54.0-point gaps cannot be attributed entirely to misleaders. The paper should foreground paired item-level comparisons and distinguish controlled effects from cross-dataset differences.

Essential reproducibility details are absent. The manuscript does not specify exact prompts, answer extraction and scoring rules for free-text and ranking questions, numerical tolerances, or how the 25.6% random baseline is calculated across heterogeneous response formats. Commercial model snapshots and the annotation/validation procedure for the new questions are also insufficiently documented. Although code and data availability is claimed, the corresponding footnote is blank in the supplied PDF. These omissions prevent a confident assessment of the reported accuracy and chance-level claims.

The explanation for table-based QA gains is not adequately isolated. This method changes both the representation and the answering model, using Qwen2.5-7B instead of the original MLLM. Consequently, its comparison with image-plus-table prompting does not establish that removing the image is the decisive cause. A same-answerer ablation, comparison with an established plot-to-table pipeline such as DePlot, and an audited subset of extracted tables would substantially strengthen the methodological contribution.

The evidence supports narrower generalization than several conclusions imply. Correction methods are tested only on three mid-sized models selected from those performing below chance, rather than the stronger evaluated systems. Several misleader categories contain only one to three instances. Experiment 2 uses just four chart pairs, and its tests across related model families do not establish generalization across charts. Category-level rankings and broad claims about MLLM susceptibility therefore need stronger qualification.

Statistical reporting is incomplete: many method-by-model comparisons are tested at p≤0.05 without a stated multiplicity treatment or confidence intervals, and repeated questions on the same chart introduce dependence that is not discussed. These concerns particularly affect the smaller redrawing gains. Overall, the study has a credible empirical core, but the preservation claim, evaluation specification, and attribution of improvements require important, feasible revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for multimodal NLP: strong chart-QA benchmark performance may conceal vulnerability to misleading visual designs. The evaluation spans 18 models, 17 misleader categories, and both synthetic and real-world charts.

The evidence supports the basic vulnerability claim. In particular, CHARTOM provides misleading and non-misleading versions of the same underlying data, and the reported average accuracy falls from 47% to 21%. This is more persuasive than comparisons between unrelated benchmarks.

The six correction strategies provide a useful empirical comparison. Table-based QA produces substantial reported gains of 15.4–19.6 percentage points on misleading charts, while redrawing significantly improves two of the three evaluated models.

The presentation is generally clear, and the paper acknowledges several meaningful limitations, including extraction errors, degraded performance on ordinary charts, chart-type assumptions, and uneven category coverage.
weaknesses: The headline claim of improving robustness without compromising ordinary-chart accuracy is not established. Table-based QA significantly reduces non-misleading accuracy for two models. Redrawing also has negative point estimates for all three models in Figure 7; failure to detect statistical significance does not establish preservation. Confidence intervals and a justified non-inferiority analysis are needed, ideally with evaluation on ChartQA, which is omitted from the correction experiment.

Important reproducibility details are missing. The manuscript does not provide exact prompts, answer parsing and scoring rules for free-text and ranking questions, the calculation of the 25.6% random baseline across heterogeneous question formats, or precise commercial-model versions. The code/data availability claim points to an empty footnote in the supplied PDF. These omissions prevent adequate verification of the central quantitative results.

The aggregate misleading-versus-non-misleading comparison mixes different datasets, questions, and chart distributions, so its 23.4-point gap cannot be attributed entirely to misleading design. CHARTOM provides stronger matched evidence, but a dedicated paired analysis with uncertainty is needed. The 42 newly annotated real-world examples also lack sufficient documentation of selection, answer validation, and annotation quality.

The correction experiments do not fully isolate the proposed mechanism. Table-based QA changes both the representation and the answering model to Qwen2.5-7B, whereas image-plus-table conditions use the original MLLM. Consequently, their comparison cannot establish that removing the image is the key cause of improvement. A controlled same-model ablation, extraction-quality assessment, and comparison with relevant plot-to-table or redraw approaches would strengthen the contribution.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence: category-level conclusions sometimes rely on one to three examples; the consistency experiment contains only four chart pairs and tests across related models rather than independent chart samples; and the proposed protective role of parametric knowledge lacks a question-only or altered-data control. Multiple significance tests are also reported without discussing multiplicity. The core empirical finding is promising, but the evaluation and reproducibility gaps require important revisions before a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant robustness problem for multimodal NLP: strong chart-QA performance does not necessarily imply reliable interpretation of misleading visualizations. Evaluating 19 models across general-purpose and chart-specialized systems provides useful descriptive breadth.

The mitigation study compares six practical inference-time approaches and evaluates their effects on both misleading and non-misleading inputs. Table-based QA yields substantial reported gains of 15.4–19.6 percentage points, while redrawing improves two of the three tested models.

The appendix provides valuable diagnostic evidence, including specialized extraction baselines, CoT experiments, and manual analyses of table and axes extraction. These analyses expose important limitations, such as poor extraction under inverted axes, dual axes, and 3D effects.

The presentation is generally clear, with illustrative examples, explicit prompts, dataset counts, and transparent discussion of several limitations. Reusing established human-evaluation resources and adding 42 real-world examples gives the study practical value.
weaknesses: The headline performance drop does not cleanly isolate misleading design. The misleading and non-misleading collections differ in source composition, content, and potentially difficulty; ChartQA also differs in question format. CHARTOM supplies 56 matched pairs, but the paper does not make paired item-level QA analysis the basis of its central claim. Such an analysis, with uncertainty estimates, is needed to distinguish the effect of misleaders from dataset differences.

Important evaluation details are missing. The paper does not specify answer normalization, free-text grading, numerical tolerances, rank scoring, or how the 25.6% random baseline is constructed across mixed question types. The new MCQs lack a documented annotation and validation protocol. Exact commercial model snapshots and a usable code/data location are also absent from the manuscript, despite the availability claim. These omissions materially limit reproducibility.

The claim of improving robustness without compromising ordinary-chart accuracy is stronger than the evidence. Table-based QA significantly reduces non-misleading accuracy for two models, and Figure 6 shows negative point estimates for redrawing on all three. Failure to detect a significant decrease on 124 instances does not establish preservation; confidence intervals and a prespecified non-inferiority margin would be more appropriate. Correction methods are not evaluated on ChartQA.

The explanation that removing the image is responsible for table-based QA gains is confounded by changing the answering model to Qwen2.5-7B. Comparing table-only and image-plus-table inputs with the same answering backbone would better isolate modality effects. The observed pipeline improvements remain useful, but claims that models ignore textual evidence are not established by aggregate accuracy alone.

Generalization is limited by the small, uneven dataset and mitigation evaluation on only three mid-sized models selected from below-random performers. Several misleader categories contain a single example, making category-level rankings especially fragile. Experiment 2 uses only four chart pairs, and its tests across related model variants do not establish generalization across charts.

Overall, this is a promising empirical contribution near the Findings threshold, but unresolved evaluation reproducibility and insufficiently controlled support for the central claims prevent a clear positive recommendation. Documenting scoring and data validation, emphasizing the existing matched-pair evidence, and narrowing the preservation and mechanism claims could substantially strengthen the submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in multimodal NLP: whether chart-understanding models remain reliable when visualization design misleads readers. Its contribution is primarily empirical, and the evaluation of 19 models across 17 misleader categories provides useful breadth.

The vulnerability finding has supporting evidence beyond comparisons with ChartQA. CHARTOM contains matched misleading and non-misleading visualizations for the same questions, with average accuracy falling from 48% to 22%. This supports a real sensitivity to misleading design.

The comparison of six inference-time interventions is useful. Table-based QA improves accuracy by 15.4–19.6 percentage points across three models, and redrawing significantly improves two models. Evaluating interventions on non-misleading charts also exposes practical trade-offs.

The appendices provide prompts, specialized extraction baselines, CoT experiments, and informative manual error analyses. The discussion acknowledges extraction failures and cases where correct answers arise despite incorrect extracted tables.
weaknesses: The headline evaluation is insufficiently specified for reproducibility. The manuscript does not explain answer normalization, free-text scoring, numerical tolerances, rank-question scoring, or how the 25.6% random baseline is calculated across heterogeneous question types. These details directly affect the central near-random-performance claim. Exact model checkpoints/API versions and a usable code/data access link are also absent from the manuscript, despite the release statement.

The aggregate accuracy gaps do not isolate misleading design: the misleading, non-misleading, and ChartQA datasets differ in questions, chart composition, and source. The matched CHARTOM results provide meaningful support, but the paper should foreground per-model paired analyses and uncertainty rather than attribute the full cross-dataset gap to misleaders.

The claim of improving robustness without compromising ordinary accuracy is too strong. Table-based QA significantly reduces non-misleading accuracy for two models, by up to 8.5 points. Redrawing also produces negative point estimates on non-misleading charts; failure to detect significance on 124 instances does not establish preservation of performance. Confidence intervals and a non-inferiority analysis would better support this claim.

The intervention comparison does not isolate why table-based QA helps. It changes both the input modality and the answering model to Qwen2.5-7B, whereas image-plus-table conditions retain the original MLLM. Consequently, the claim that models ignore the table in favor of the image is not established by these comparisons. A controlled comparison using the same answering model is needed.

Several broader conclusions exceed the available evidence. Experiment 2 uses only four chart pairs, with significance assessed across models that include related checkpoints; this offers limited evidence for generalization across charts. Three misleader categories contain just one instance each. Mitigations are evaluated only on three models selected from those performing below chance, leaving their effectiveness on stronger models unresolved.

The new 42-example dataset lacks a documented annotation-validation procedure, and the statistical reporting omits confidence intervals and discussion of multiple comparisons. Overall, the paper contains a promising empirical contribution, but unresolved scoring, reproducibility, and inference issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for multimodal NLP: reliable chart question answering under misleading visual design. Evaluating both vulnerability and practical mitigation makes the contribution useful beyond benchmark reporting.

The evaluation covers 19 models, 17 distortion categories, established human-evaluation resources, and 42 newly annotated real-world examples. The paired misleading/non-misleading examples in CHARTOM provide particularly useful evidence.

Comparing six inference-time interventions yields an actionable result: table-based QA improves misleading-chart accuracy by 15.4–19.6 percentage points across three tested models. Evaluating effects on ordinary charts and including DePlot, MatCha, and chain-of-thought baselines strengthens the study.

The appendices provide valuable diagnostic analysis of table and axes extraction. They explicitly document extraction failures, correct answers obtained from incorrect tables, and distortions that persist in tabular form, avoiding an overly simple account of why mitigation works.
weaknesses: The headline accuracy drops compare datasets with different chart distributions, questions, and answer formats. They therefore do not isolate the effect of misleading design. CHARTOM provides a matched comparison and supports the qualitative vulnerability claim, but its paired results should be analyzed explicitly, with uncertainty estimates, rather than using the aggregate 23.8- and 53.8-point gaps as evidence of the distortion effect.

Evaluation details are insufficient for confident reproduction. The manuscript does not specify answer normalization, numerical tolerances, ranking criteria, or how the 25.6% random baseline combines MCQ, free-text, and ranking questions. Commercial model snapshots and validation procedures for the new MCQs are also unspecified. Although code and data release is claimed, no repository link is identifiable in the manuscript, and CHARTOM requires contacting its authors.

Preserving non-misleading-chart accuracy is not established. Table-based QA significantly reduces accuracy for two models, by up to 8.5 points. Redrawing also produces negative point estimates for all three models; nonsignificance does not demonstrate preservation. The abstract's framing should be narrowed, and confidence intervals or a noninferiority analysis would better support this central objective.

The explanation that removing the image drives table-based QA gains is confounded by switching the answering model to Qwen2.5-7B. A controlled comparison using the same answering model with and without the image is needed to distinguish modality effects from differences in reasoning ability. Correction experiments also cover only three models selected from below the random baseline, leaving effectiveness on stronger models unresolved.

Experiment 2 uses only four chart pairs and treats responses from 19 related models as the paired observations for significance testing. This does not establish generalization across charts or independent model populations. Likewise, several per-distortion conclusions rest on only one to three examples and should be presented as observations about those instances.

Overall, the paper contains a promising empirical contribution, but unresolved scoring and reproducibility details, confounded comparisons, and an unsupported accuracy-preservation claim prevent a clear Findings recommendation. These concerns are addressable through clearer reporting, controlled analyses, and narrower claims.
